en: One who comments on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* will surely quickly understand the true permanence [of the Buddha-nature]; that he has attained a lifespan of eighty years is merely because he responds to the needs of sentient beings.

This means that his mind is free from doubt. As for the instruction to "promptly dispatch a messenger to inspire the aspiration for the Way," it means one should send such a messenger at this very moment.
"Faith is that which causes the sentient beings for whom Śrīmālā acts to always understand the intent of the Way.
'Now is precisely the time' means that today is precisely the time for those sentient beings for whom Śrīmālā acts to always attain understanding."
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (or *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*) explains the dispatching of this letter.
It briefly extols the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.
The phrasing is concise and brief, hence it is called "abridged";
yet its principles are pervasive and its meanings complete, such that the words are immeasurable.
This dispatches [the message] to the messenger; by presenting this letter, one expresses gratitude for their intention.
"Ayuja Country" is the name of a district or town;
this is what it means.
With joyful hearts,
those in the land of Qin who are seven years of age or older are all transformed by the Mahāyāna,
their minds constantly focused on liberation.
For this reason, it was named accordingly;
that the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* was respectfully bestowed as a treatise on the eternal abiding [of the Dharma] is truly worthy of high esteem.
The ultimate name for this is "reverence.
Because one receives and presents it to another person, it is called "bestowing" (授).
There may also be a formal ritual for the bestowal of books.
"Grasping [the book] and bowing with the upper body leaning forward and the lower body receiving it—this is the ritual for receiving a book; therefore, it is called 'respectfully receiving.
Regarding 'receiving with joy upon the crown of the head':
the internal state of feeling is termed 'joy.'"
Because one prostrates and receives [the teaching], it is called "receiving upon the crown" (*ting shou*).
Alternatively, within the body, the crown is the most honored and thus preeminent;
among the ways of receiving the Path, this is the foremost.
Because one receives [the teaching] with the strongest faith and a heart of profound reverence, it is called "this book"; thus, it is said that one "receives it upon the crown of the head.
As for "reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding":

just as one repeats a statement three times to ensure its strength, one thereby recognizes any flaws; by consulting the written text and investigating the words, one understands what they signify—hence, it is called "reading and reciting."

Furthermore, to be able to receive the elegant phrasing and harmonious sentences, to recite them with understanding of the words and mastery of the names, to take them into one's heart, to receive them through oral transmission, to remember them without forgetting—this is what constitutes "retention" (*dhāraṇī*).
Since such a thing has never existed before, it gives rise to a sense of rare wonder.
The first two lines of the following verse were spoken to Caṇḍila. Why was this so?
In this letter from Cāṇḍī, who honors her parents, she exhorts Śrīmālā to be reverent in her three karmas.
Because the Tathāgata now respectfully upholds her instructions,
he first addresses her with these verses.
Regarding the phrase "I heard the Buddha's voice":
because the voice was transmitted through written records, it is said that "I heard.
Furthermore, by following the written records, one can give rise to clear understanding and attain a vivid realization of the Buddha's voice.
Because one hears from the mouths of one's parents the sound of the Buddha’s teaching that he is eternally abiding,
one uses these words as an ear;
this is something that has never before occurred in the world.
I have said that since my birth into this world, I have never heard of such a person as this.
This also clarifies that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) arise and perish in alternation,
whereas the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and serenely illuminating.
The arising and ceasing of the myriad objects cannot add suffering or joy;
nothing can alter this.
How could such a thing have ever existed in the world?
The following two lines intend to follow the teaching and receive its instruction:
as stated in the scripture, the Tathāgata is eternally abiding; being free from emptiness, he is called "Real" (zhen).
He who is utterly devoid of name and reality is [the Tathāgata].
I should cultivate the three types of action as an offering.
The second verse silently entreats the Buddha;
the first two lines constitute this silent entreaty.
The latter two phrases are a request to the Buddha.
"Yǎng" (仰) means to look up with reverence;
"wéi" (惟) means to contemplate.
The following explains the matter of contemplation.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared for the sake of all those in the world who possess the karmic affinity;
I am among the number of those with such affinity.
"You should also show compassion by appearing within the inner palace;
you must certainly allow me to see you.
[The following] verses clarify how he responded to this inspiration.
"At the very moment this thought arose" means at the very moment he gave rise to the thought of reverent contemplation.
"The Buddha appeared within the palace" refers to [the manifestation therein].
To manifest that which is eternally abiding and free from the realm of birth and death, it appears within emptiness.
"Universal" (Pu) means that its light shines impartially; thus it is called universal.
The light emitted from the Buddha’s body is called "pure radiance" because it can extinguish all darkness;
it may also manifest the body of true permanence.
Because it removes the defilement of doubt and hesitation, it is called "universally emitting pure light.
Regarding the manifestation of the incomparable body:
because the light illuminates and clearly reveals a physical form that is uniquely marvelous and unsurpassed by any other marks, it is called the "incomparable body."
He may also possess the thirty-two marks;
because worldly appearances cannot equal them, they are called "incomparable.
As for Śrīmālā and her retinue:
This clarifies that the offering of the three types of action (trikarma) should be understood as previously stated.
It demonstrates that prostrating at the feet in person is the devotion of the bodily action (kāyakarma),
while a pure mind is the reverence of the mental action (manaskarma).
"Exclaiming the Buddha’s merits" refers to the verbal act of praise.
From the passage "From the Tathāgata’s wondrously colored body" onwards is the second major section, which elucidates the actual substance of the sutra.
Within this, there are two sections that clarify the meaning.
From the beginning up to the "Vehicle of the Ultimate Truth" (paramārthayāna), the essence and practice of the vehicle are elucidated.
From the passage "The World-Honored One [taught] the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" onwards...
Because the Vehicle does not arise in isolation, but arises from conditions;
thus, the eight chapters below all clarify the realm of the Vehicle.
This is why the first chapter begins with the fifteenth chapter by extolling the merits of the Buddha.
This is intended to cause the arising of the virtuous causes for taking refuge through the three karmas, thereby transcending the world;
it may also be seen as an expression of admiration conveyed through the written word.
As for the phrase "the Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body," this first praises the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
The Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) appears as a Buddha in accordance with the Dharma to transform sentient beings;
Śākyamuni is likewise, and for this reason he is called the Tathāgata.
Alternatively, there is another interpretation: because he has always come according to reality to attain perfect enlightenment, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Shared Teaching explains that by realizing the path of reality through emptiness, one attains equal and perfect enlightenment;
because the fruit is viewed in light of the cause, one is called the Tathāgata.
As for the "wondrous form-body":
Because this form manifests from the realm of reality, it is called "wondrous form.
Because it takes form as its substance, it is called the "wondrous form-body" (rūpakāya).
There is nothing in the world that can equal it.
The forms of the world are produced by the influence of fetters and so forth;
the body of the Tathāgata appears in accordance with sentient beings, and for this reason it is said that there is nothing equal to it.
Regarding "incomparable," the preceding statement says there is nothing equal to it.
Because there is nothing with which it can be equaled, nor anything to which it can be compared, it is said to be "without peer.
As for "inconceivable":
because he manifests himself at various heights—whether three feet or sixteen feet tall—and yet one cannot see the crown of his head, it is called "inconceivable."
Regarding "form is inexhaustible":
this is intended to clarify that while the true source is never lost, the myriad phenomena manifest simultaneously; thus it is called "inexhaustible.
These five phrases all praise the reasons for the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The initial praise of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is intended to indicate that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) is eternally abiding and wondrously transcendent beyond the realm of words; thus, it is difficult to awaken to.
However, when the sixteen-foot radiant form appears in the world, understanding arises easily.
For this reason, the response-body is praised first.
Desiring to trace the marks in order to infer the source,
he next clarifies the True Body (dharmakāya).
The same applies to wisdom as well.
There are also five phrases that do not differ from the preceding sutra;
because the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) are abbreviated, it simply says "it is likewise.
Regarding "all phenomena are eternally abiding":
Because the myriad dharmas are fully replete, they are called "all-encompassing.
Because they are not tilted by arising or ceasing, they are termed "eternally abiding.
Their virtue transcends that of all sages.
Therefore, one pays homage.
"Subduing the faults and evils of the mind" praises liberation.
The preceding section clarified that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and does not perish throughout kalpas;
yet, this attainment of the eternal fruit must necessarily have its cause.
Because the fruit has been fully explained, the following verse praises liberation.
Regarding "subduing the faults and evils of the mind":
this means the total exhaustion of mental evils.
Regarding "the four kinds of the body": [as follows].
Because physical form is subject to decay and death,
the mind possesses greed, hatred, and delusion,
and the body undergoes birth, aging, sickness, and death.
It is said that the mind surpasses the body in four ways.
As for "having reached the stage difficult to subdue," this is precisely because the afflictions of form and mind have been exhausted, and one has attained the fruit of Buddhahood through the Path.
Arising and ceasing cannot add suffering or pleasure;
because nothing can move it, it is called the "ground difficult to subdue.
This may also be verified by the following passage.
There are two types of afflictions:
the four abodes of ignorance and the ignorance regarding karma within the three realms. This is discussed in terms of activity.
The higher stages are explained in terms of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the subduing of mental faults and evils, the three [mental] grounds are abandoned;
as for "and the body," one should say "the three [bodily grounds]."
Fourth, their speech consists merely of superficial and abbreviated discourse.
Regarding the body, there are three deficiencies; regarding speech, there are four types of silence.
These are the karmas produced by the four abodes of the three realms.
Because the soil of karma is severed through the extinction of delusions,
we shall discuss it in terms of karma.
As for those who have reached the stage of "Difficult to Subdue":
This statement means that although the delusions of ignorance have been exhausted, one has merely reached the point of "crossing over.
Unless one employs the diamond-like mind as the seed of unimpeded wisdom for liberation, these delusions will inevitably cause the crown of the head to fall;
therefore, it is called the "Stage Difficult to Subdue" (Durjayā-bhūmi).
"Knowing all *tathatā* (suchness)" next clarifies *prajñā*. Above,
it was clarified that through the exhaustion of all defilements, one attains that fruit of permanence.
Alternatively, because the cessation of existence has a specific method that is neither ignorance nor aversion, it is explained next.
In this region, *er yan* (爾炎) is called the "mother of wisdom" (*jñānamātṛ*);
it may also be said that wisdom itself is that *er yan*.
That which is "er" (爾) is the ultimate truth;
that which is "yan" (炎) is the conventional truth. Why is this so?

Now, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is suchness (*tathatā*), the fixed standard throughout past and present; the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is provisional and deceptive, like pulling away a burning flame so as not to grasp it—this is merely the perspective of wisdom.
From here below, the three dharmas mentioned above are again summarized.
The wise one binds all knowledges (*jñāna*).
The body is the binding of the mastery of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); it is the binding and liberation of deliverance (*vimukti*).
It is that which gathers and sustains all phenomena (*dharma*).
When these three dharmas are complete, all virtues reach their ultimate perfection;
because what is once attained is eternally firm and does not perish even at the end of an eon,
it is said that they "comprehend and sustain all dharmas."
Homage to the One Beyond Measure.
He has come once more desiring to sweep away all traces [of doubt].
At that time, the assembly fully realized the principles of the Buddha-ground’s merits as praised by Śrīmālā.
Therefore, I now pay homage to you who have brushed away all prior traces;
you transcend my capacity for measurement, standing alone and peerless beyond all comparison, such that no analogy can describe you.
The fruit of Buddhahood accumulates myriad virtues; because its principle and path transcend verbal expression, it is called "boundless Dharma.
That which the Tathāgata has attained cannot be fathomed by inferior sentiments, and is therefore called "inconceivable."
Furthermore, the various preceding phrases may also be counted as prostrations.
Therefore, this verse truly refers to the tracks [of practice];
when it says, "I now prostrate," it means this.
This surpasses my lamentation.
Out of compassion for those below, you desire to clarify this request for protection;
O Ānanda, take pity on me and shield me with your grace.
Now, regarding the five phrases praising the Buddha’s wholesome dharmas, it is said that they quickly increase;
because this basis of goodness brings forth bodhi, it is called a "seed.
This refers to the present life, the current body.
And for those born hereafter,
may they always be gathered and sustained within the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Having long established this, I have now fulfilled their request according to the Tathāgata’s will.
The preceding two sections have established [the Buddhas] as teachers;
now, this section clarifies the reason why they act as protectors throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, as for those who have transgressed:
If one were to protect only the present and future, it would not necessarily be so;
therefore, by citing past transgressions, one guards against those yet to come.
This is how one establishes oneself with long-term vigilance and stability.
From your previous lives onward, you have been enabled to escape the heavy sufferings of the three miserable realms; this is called "peace.
You have been enabled to cause your roots of goodness and meritorious virtues to flourish; this is called "establishment."
In a previous life, I opened your mind because you delighted in awakening to the Mahāyāna; thus it was said that you were "opened and awakened.
Now, I again embrace you in the present.
It shall be the same for your future births as well.
"It is the same as your past and present [merit].
Regarding "I have already performed meritorious deeds," the following clarifies the request for a prediction by again citing the virtues of the three periods of time mentioned above.
Regarding "that which has already produced clarity in the past":
this refers to the present life and the remainder of future lives.
Such are the roots of all virtues.
This summarizes all the various merits of the three periods mentioned above;
that which is capable of acting as the cause for the fruit is called the "basis" (mūla).
"I only pray that you will graciously accept me."
This correctly clarifies the request for a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because one wishes to see the fruit that is embraced by this very cause,
it says, "I pray that you will see [me] being embraced."
It is not so; rather, she desires to sweep away [defilements] and seek the protection of two lifetimes to repay the traces of the establishment of peace throughout the three times.
At that time, from the point where Śrīmālā prostrated herself before the Buddha, he granted her the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), fulfilling her request.
Furthermore, there are two reasons why the prediction (vyākaraṇa) is bestowed here in this section:
first, to introduce the subsequent text;
second, to inspire the assembly at that time to cultivate the conditions for rebirth [in the Pure Land].
For this reason, he grants the prediction.
As for your praise of the Tathāgata’s true merits,
you have brought forth the excellence of the aforementioned merits praised in the Buddha.
It is called a "faculty" (*indriya*) because it is capable of bringing about the fruit of Buddhahood;
this clarifies the mindfulness of the proximate cause.
From the section on "immeasurable" [qualities] below, it clarifies the mindfulness of the proximate fruit.
Among gods and humans, he is a sovereign king;
this is the fruit of the sixth heaven.
Why does he dwell here? It is to clarify that by abiding above, one transforms those below—just as grass bends downward when the wind blows. Thus it is.
He dispelled doubts regarding all places of birth;
at that time, the assembly took him to be the sixth heavenly king,
for they shared his wrong views and were addicted to the five sensory objects.
It is said that one shall always see me appearing before them and praising them, no different from now.
Why [speak of] false views and dissipation? "Now there is this world;
what more could there be hereafter? and so forth.
The second section records the distant causes and distant fruits.
There are two kinds of fruits:
the general and the specific.
The specific epithet "Universal Radiance" (Pulguang) clarifies the general title below.
Second, its land is recorded;
therein, two sections clarify the meaning.
From the beginning up to the paths of unwholesome karma, this is called clarifying that which is to be eliminated.
The sentient beings of that land obtain [these results] through their inferior [conduct].
As for that Buddha-land:
Judging from the present in view of the future,
Samantaprabha is for their sake.
"Free from all evils" means...
Within the Pure Land, there are no four evil realms;
there are only devas and humans.
Furthermore, among them, there are no fruits such as old age, sickness, decline, affliction, or the suffering of unpleasantness.
The passage beginning with "Therefore, there is no such retribution of suffering" clarifies that the name of those evil paths of action does not exist;
for this reason, there are no bitter fruits of suffering such as old age, illness, and so forth.
From "those sentient beings of that second land" onwards,
it clarifies their virtues;
as for "physical form, strength, and lifespan":
"Old age, sickness, and the affliction of decay" is the opposite of the former [suffering of change].
"The pleasures of the five desires" is the opposite of the former [suffering of not obtaining what one wishes for].
Those sentient beings who are exclusively of the Mahāyāna are called "exclusive" because,
contrary to the aforementioned state, they are free from all evil realms.
These are the sentient beings who cultivate roots of goodness.
Conversely, there is likewise no mention of unwholesome or evil karmic paths;
all such factors are gathered therein,
and through these conditions, they are reborn together in the Pure Land.
The aspiration for that land is precisely the purport of the prophecy;
it is superior to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in its excellence of praising the Buddha’s virtues.
The Tathāgata then bestowed upon him the prediction that he would become a Buddha in the Pure Land of Universal Radiance,
adorned with lapis lazuli; yet this wondrous fruit cannot be attained through mere passive inaction.
Now, to achieve the essential goal, one must cultivate the causes that lead to the fruit;
among the myriad practices of these causes, the precepts must come first.
This is the second chapter, which elucidates the ten great vows.
This chapter clarifies its meaning in three sections.
The first explains the preliminary methods for undertaking the ten precepts.
The second, beginning from the words "World-Honored One, from this day forward," elucidates the essential nature of the ten precepts.
The third section, from the phrase "From the Dharma-Lord, the World-Honored One" through the end of the chapter, clarifies the evidence for faith.
"Reverence" specifically clarifies the desire to receive the precepts;
it refers to the cultivation of respect through bodily action.
Regarding the requirement to stand:
according to the essential rules for receiving the precepts, one must kneel with the right knee on the ground;
the reason for standing now is as follows.
The Buddha was dwelling in mid-air while Śrīmālā remained on the ground.
Had she been kneeling with one knee raised, the space between them would have been so vast that the path of speech would have been severed and the sound of their voices cut off.
Now, wishing to ensure that their words and sounds could reach one another, she stood upright.
It may also signify that one is certainly able to practice them.
Regarding the "receiving of the ten great vows," the lower [category] refers to receiving them as the observance of precepts.
The reason for this is that it is intended to clarify that precepts are acquired through the act of undertaking them; thus,
the term "undertaking" is used to designate the precepts.
The "Great" [precepts] refer to the precepts received by Śrāvakas, which last for the duration of a single lifetime;
these precepts ultimately culminate in the fruit of Buddhahood.
Alternatively, it may be said that Śrāvakas merely restrain their body and speech.
Because the Bodhisattva brings the three karmas to rest, he is called "Great.
From the passage concerning the World-Honored One downward,
the text correctly elucidates ten points of reception, which are explained in four sections.
Regarding the first precept: it is easy to receive but difficult to maintain;
therefore, the first "receiving" clarifies the solemn vow of maintenance.
The subsequent four "receivings" clarify the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint).
Next, there are four precepts that clarify the precept of gathering in sentient beings;
the final one among them is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
From this day forward, beginning with the reception of these precepts:
This continues until the conclusion of the vow for enlightenment.
As for those who receive the precepts,
they do not give rise to a mind of transgression regarding the nine lesser precepts they have received.
Why is it said only that one does not give rise to a mind of transgression?
It is easy to commit a transgression with a mind of desire, for such a mind is clear;
however, a transgression involving form is difficult.
That which is easy is not transgressed;
one should know that what is difficult is likewise maintained.
Furthermore, the mind may be regarded as the root, while body and speech are the branches.
It is simply said that one can know [the state of the precepts] by observing how the mind governs body and speech.
People understand that this one precept is the general basis from which the nine subsequent precepts arise;
if one violates those nine lower precepts, [it constitutes a violation of this one].
This precept is such that there is no distinct evil counterpart to its violation,
nor does a general evil come to invade it. Furthermore,
another interpretation holds that this precept possesses its own distinct intrinsic nature.
Why is this so? For example, if one intends to give rise to a mind of anger, one violates this precept;
when actual wrath arises and one reviles another, one then breaks the third precept. The same applies to the remaining eight categories.
"Those who do not give rise to pride toward their elders and superiors" clarifies the respect shown to those above.
"Elders and superiors" refers to those whose virtue is lofty and whose capacity is far-reaching; because they contemplate and attain mastery over all things, they are called elders and superiors.
It is not that the years need not be accounted for;

rather, toward one's elders and superiors, one ought precisely to cultivate reverence, provide sustenance, and inquire about what they have not yet heard. To speak of "dark intercalary months" [in this context] is improper.
If one exalts oneself and treats others with contempt, the Dharma-water will not moisten them.
It is like rain falling from a high peak; because it does not fall from on high, it is said that he does not give rise to a mind of pride.
"Not giving rise to a mind of anger" clarifies his treatment of those below him.
If one feels anger toward a person, there is a separation from the object;
how then could one reach them through the Way to uproot their suffering? Therefore, it is said that one does not give rise to a mind of resentment.
The preceding precept clarified not giving rise to a mind of pride.
To request the Dharma, to cherish this illumination, and to transform sentient beings through practice—this is all that constitutes [the purpose].
Regarding the "totality of another's bodily form":
a body measuring eight chi in height is called a "body" (kāya).
The description of "jade-like brilliance" refers to the color of the sun;
"birds, horses, and the seven treasures" refers to various implements beyond those [specifically named].
As for "not giving rise to a mind of illness":
Now, one who acts as a bodhisattva takes the celebration of all beings as their concern.
If they harbor malice or envy toward others,
how can they bestow virtue and happiness upon people?
Therefore, it is said that one should not give rise to a mind of affliction regarding internal and external phenomena. Among these,
the head, eyes, limbs, and joints are called "internal."
The seven treasures constitute the external [objects].
Regarding "not giving rise to a mind of stinginess":
this refers to not giving rise to a mind of envy toward the wealth and goods of others.
"How is it that today you are so clear-sighted as to be free from stinginess?
It is for this reason that you do not harbor envy toward others.
"World-Honored One, from this day forward," [he said].
The second section clarifies the precept of gathering in sentient beings (*sattvārthasamgrāhaka-śīla*).
The first two vows are the instruments for gathering in beings;
the latter two vows concern the sentient beings who are gathered in.
Regarding the statement that one does not personally receive or possess wealth and goods:
because a bodhisattva accumulates wealth as vast as the sands of the Ganges with the sole intention of benefiting sentient beings,
it is said that they do not act for their own sake.
"Whatever one receives is entirely for the sake of maturing [others]" means that because people lack food and clothing, they have no means to practice virtue; therefore,
it is necessary to bring them to maturity.
Regarding the statement that one does not practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) for one's own sake:
this is intended to clarify that among persons there is a distinction between the present and the future, as well as a difference in terms of excellence and inferiority.
Therefore, the former [category] exclusively encompasses those in the present.
If these sentient beings come as a multitude of evil transformed by this illumination,
it is because the Bodhisattva has accumulated merit to benefit others; thus,
he says that he does not act for his own sake.
"One whose mind is not stained by craving" means one whose mind is free from greed.
"One whose mind has no sense of satiety" means...
The compassion born of attachment and views does not transform beings universally.
The preceding passage clarifies that by being free from grasping, one is able to provide pervasive and unimpeded nourishment;
hence, it speaks of a mind that is never weary or satisfied.
Regarding the unimpeded mind:
because it eliminates anger and harmonizes with others to transform sentient beings,
it is said that the unimpeded mind gathers in and sustains all beings.
Furthermore, because he does not have a mind of attachment, he differs from ordinary people;
because he has no mind of insatiability, he differs from the śrāvakas.
Since the Great Being practices by forgetting both, it is called the unimpeded mind.
Because one takes up the position of a Mahāyāna practitioner following those who preceded one,
it is said that one "gathers in sentient beings.
From the words "From this day forward" onwards, the text correctly clarifies the gathering of sentient beings as the aforementioned equipment.
Those who are bound in secret confinement refer to those subjected to shackles, stocks, and other forms of restraint;
fearing excessive prolixity, I shall describe them here in brief and general terms.
This refers to various perils and hardships.
"Desiring security" means causing those sentient beings to be exempt from suffering and calamity.
Regarding those who benefit through righteous means:
for those without fathers, he provides the sheltering protection of compassion;
for those without sons, he manifests as a servant to nourish and support them.
May those who are bound in confinement be freed from the suffering of shackles and fetters;
may those who are ill find their vital spirits harmonized and refreshed by the celestial deities.
Because one benefits others through these four matters,
it is said that "one enriches them with meaning. Furthermore,
it may also mean that one instructs and guides them by means of the Mahāyāna so that they may be liberated from birth and death.
"Speaking for the benefit of others through righteousness" clarifies that he gathers in virtuous beings and rescues those of the present.
"From this day forward," and so forth.
This clarifies the future suffering of evil sentient beings.
Those who "capture" are so called because they ensnare flying birds with nets;
those who "rear" refer to those who feed and nourish running beasts.
"Those with various evil vows" refers to the sixteen types of evil vows.
"Never abandoning them even for a moment" means...
Because the Great Being does not depart from sentient beings but teaches them by means of the Mahāyāna, it is said that he does not abandon them even for a moment.
As for the phrase "the power of my virtue and time," it is because sentient beings are boundless and can never be exhausted.
This is the time when one makes the vow to attain the power of the Dharma-body.
Because these sentient beings are not uniform, the Bodhisattva refers to them as "this and that" (*tatra tatra*).
As for "seeing these sentient beings":
If they are evil persons,

As it says below: "Because one has gone forth by relying on the Buddha and has received full ordination as one who has gone forth by relying on the Mahāyāna."
Therefore, the majestic ethical discipline (*vinaya*) of the Mahāyāna is designated by the name of the *vinaya* of the Hīnayāna;
for this reason, it is said that "vinaya" is itself the training of the Mahāyāna.
This refers to those who have gone forth in reliance upon the Buddha.
This should be the fifth chapter-gate.
"One who has received full ordination" is the sixth chapter-gate.
Citing these two phrases establishes that there is no separate minor Vinaya;
this Vinaya is the Hīnayāna,
yet it is precisely the Mahāyāna Vinaya.
It even states that one may enter the Mahāyāna and then undergo the renunciation and full ordination (*upasampadā*) of the Hīnayāna.
Therefore, for an Arhat, there is no separate Hīnayāna renunciation and full ordination.
Why is this so? Because the *vinaya* for those who have left home in the Hīnayāna is entirely the *vinaya* for those who have left home in the Mahāyāna;
as stated below, Arhats rely on the Tathāgata, and because those of the Mahāyāna leave home and receive full ordination [therein].
According to the fifth chapter on the pre-ordination of those following the Tathāgata,
and the sixth chapter on the full ordination,
one should measure each finger-breadth individually.
However, because the preceding section established that there is no distinction through the act of lifting and receiving,
and since the matter of the Vinaya is something that must be known,
this chapter does not compose a separate text.
That an Arhat takes refuge in the Buddha is the first chapter-gate.
That an Arhat possesses fear is the second chapter-gate.
First, I shall explain the second.
For what reason does an Arhat experience fear?
Therefore, it is said below that one dwells with the perception of dread toward all formations (*saṃskāra*), just as if a person were approaching with a drawn sword intent on harming oneself.
Therefore, there is fear.
Within the realm where all are without practice, there exists the antidote, the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
This is because, outside the three realms, the untainted path has not yet been cultivated.
Regarding the statement "dwelling in the perception of fear toward all formations," this is a case of referring to the cause by means of the fruit.
It is like a person who has not yet compared [the world] to the sword of ignorance and afflictions.
The metaphor of "receiving" illustrates the cycle of birth and death through transformation;
"clinging" illustrates the afflictions as the cause that can bring about the fruit of birth and death.
This is intended to clarify that when a person grasps a sword, they are able to inflict injury upon things.
Because the chapter on the fruit of suffering states that [suffering] can pervasively afflict even Arhats—
just as if a person were brandishing a sword and coming to harm oneself—
for this reason, Arhats do not possess ultimate bliss.
Why is this? The following explains the second chapter.
Regarding "relying on one who does not seek reliance":
it means seeking refuge only in the Buddha and not seeking to rely upon material things.
Furthermore, because the Buddha is one who does not seek a person upon whom to rely, but rather relies upon the Buddha himself,
it is said that he relies [on the Buddha] and does not seek reliance on a person.
From here below, the following chapter presents an analogy.
Those sentient beings who are without a refuge are likened to arhats;
those who experience various terrors are likened to arhats who still possess fear and thus seek a place of refuge.
Just as one who relies on others does not seek their own refuge,
so it is with the Arhat:
though he dwells among sentient beings who possess fear, he remains unafraid.
Regarding "because of fear, one relies upon the Tathāgata":
it means that because of various fears, one relies [on him] in every situation where there is fear.
Thus, one seeks refuge in the Buddha’s great power—
namely, the World-Honored One, the Arhats, and those below them, including the Pratyekabuddhas. Second,
the distinct assemblies regarding the fruits [of practice] enter into the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna).
Before explaining that [the state] is not ultimate, it is first stated that there is still fear.
This refers to the Arhat for whom the phenomena of further birth have not been exhausted;
although the afflictions—the phenomena of taking birth—have been exhausted, the ignorance-ground (avidyā-āvāsabhūmi) of the triple-world cycle of birth and death remains.
Alternatively, because one has not yet discarded and transformed the body that constitutes the basis for the realms,
the body of the three realms is still referred to as "with remainder.
This explains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
With respect to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), there are five [knowledges] that emerge from the completion of the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
with respect to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), there are four knowledges that emerge because what was to be done has been accomplished.
When abbreviated by time, these are designated as two knowledges.
How is this known?

It is because the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)—whether regarding the exhaustion of birth and death or the completion of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)—is established through the ultimate perfection of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
It is precisely because it is established by means of the cause that is the holy life that birth and death are exhausted.
By means of the knowledge of non-arising, one emerges having completed what was to be done.
"Having completed what was to be done" means that because the untainted [qualities] are fully perfected, there is no further arising;
thus, a future body will not be born again.
It is precisely because it is accomplished through causes;
or, because [defilements] are exhausted and no longer arise, the remaining portion of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is fulfilled.
As for that which is impure, because the remainder of the three realms has not yet been accomplished, the essence of the fruit is impure.
This negates the second wisdom.
Regarding "the matter not being consummated": it means that the task of severing birth and death is not yet consummated.
Furthermore, because one must still rely on and cultivate superior resolve (*adhimukti*),
it is said that "there is yet more to be done.
This refutes the third wisdom.
"Because they have not yet crossed over to the other shore" means that because they have not yet encountered the transformation of death and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*),
they must further eliminate delusions and exhaust the fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, it is said that "there is something to be abandoned."
This refutes the fourth knowledge.
Because it is not abandoned, the last one is briefly cited as an example.
It refutes the fifth, the unconditioned, because it is not ultimate.
This means that they are far removed from the realm of Nirvana.
Why is this? The first five phrases of the second section correctly negate the ultimate fruit of the Two Vehicles;
from here below, it figuratively negates [the attainment of] Buddhahood.
Why is this? Because the four types of knowledge of the śrāvakas are neither ultimate nirvāṇa nor final;
this clarifies below that only the Tathāgata attains *parinirvāṇa*, for he has eliminated all deficiencies and perfected all meritorious qualities.
It is said that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is ultimately fulfilled [only in Buddhahood];
because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas do not accomplish all merits,
their knowledge of exhaustion is not yet complete.
If that is so, why does the text speak of "ultimate" and then say that "the ultimate of verbal expression" refers to the Buddha’s skillful means?
This is a negation of exhaustion.
Herein, it negates his four types of knowledge.

For what reason? Because the path to nirvāṇa is understood through the sounds of verbal expression, and because śrāvakas cherish nirvāṇa with such fervent attachment, all four types of wisdom are deprived of their specific names and designated by the single name "nirvāṇa.
This applies to everyone from the Tathāgata downward.
This deprives [the practitioner] of the second holy life (brahmacarya),
for it establishes that only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa and accomplishes immeasurable merit,
whereas Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas accomplish only conditioned attainments.
The holy life (brahmacarya) does not stand.
What was said previously regarding its establishment was the Buddha’s skillful means (upāya).
Only those from the Tathāgata downward [possess it].
Third, it supersedes that which has already been accomplished.
Because the Tathāgata has attained parinirvāṇa and perfected inconceivable merit,
that which was to be done has been accomplished.
Because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have accomplished inconceivable merit,
that which they had not yet accomplished [in the past] is what was referred to as "accomplished" by the Buddha as a skillful means.
Only those from the Tathāgata downward possess the fourth [knowledge], the knowledge of not undergoing further existence;
only the Tathāgata attains parinirvāṇa.

All faults that ought to be severed—the afflictions of all birth and death—are completely eliminated without remainder because he has accomplished the second purity; thus, he does not undergo further existence.
As for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, because they possess residual faults despite their purity, they cannot avoid undergoing further existence.
The former statement that one will not undergo further existence was the Buddha’s skillful means;
it applies only to those below the level of the Tathāgata.
The fifth is the phrase "seizing nirvāṇa.
Because the essence of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is the ultimate principle that transcends the three vehicles,
it is said that he is gazed upon by all sentient beings, surpassing the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles.
Therefore, one should know that the fruits attained by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are far removed from the realm of Great Nirvāṇa;
this too should be understood as a skillful means of the Buddha.
However, because this specific statement is missing,
it must be established by the subsequent text.
When it says "the Arhat and Pratyekabuddha observe," it refers to the four preceding types of knowledge.
"Emancipation" refers to the fifth phrase.
The culmination of the four knowledges establishes the meaning of the preceding observation.
"The place of rest" refers to—
Following the previous explanation, the general summary of the four wisdoms and nirvana as liberation states that these two fruits are ultimate; however,
this too is the Tathāgata’s expedient teaching of provisional meaning.
This establishes the fifth preceding phrase.
It is the phrase concerning *nirvāṇa*.
Alternatively, the first five phrases may exclude the four wisdoms as well as the existence of *nirvāṇa*.
From the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas downward, this constitutes unconditioned nirvana (*asaṃskṛta-nirvāṇa*).
As for the section beginning with "For what reason," it is the third major section, which explains the differences.
Within this, there are two sections clarifying the meaning:
first, the clarification of the two kinds of birth-and-death;
second, the clarification of the two kinds of afflictions.
Why is there a distinction between superior and inferior in *nirvāṇa*, and a differentiation between the two kinds of fourfold wisdom?
It is because, as stated below, there are two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has often taught that for the Śrāvaka and the two vehicles, the fourfold wisdom of *nirvāṇa* is ultimate.
Now, Śrīmālā’s statement is not true. Why?
Because two statements are contradictory.
If Śrīmālā’s words are correct, [the other must be false].
If the Tathāgata were speaking falsely,
then Queen Śrīmālā would be speaking in vain;
if the Tathāgata’s words are correct, then Śrīmālā is merely repeating them.
Since these two teachings are contradictory, they should not both be accepted as final.
Therefore, it is stated below that there are two kinds of birth-and-death;
because the Śrīmālā-sūtra speaks of both sides, it is said to be not ultimate.
The Tathāgata speaks of only one [vehicle], and thus it is called ultimate.
Although the traces appear contradictory, they do not in fact conflict; therefore, this is called "resolving differences.
From the passage beginning with "from death by fragmentation" onwards...
This clarifies the reasons why the Tathāgata’s teaching is ultimate;
it does not mean that all afflictions and below are not so explained.
It specifically explains the reason why the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra is said to be non-ultimate.
Both sides possess their own meaning without losing the central tenet.
What are these two? The first is death by way of segments (pariccheda-maraṇa).
Within the three realms, from the upper limit of eighty thousand years down to the lower limit of ten years,
there are distinct differences in the physical bodies and retributions of beings.
Second, outside the three realms, because it involves a transformation prior to the final [death], it is called "transformation-death" (pariṇāmi-cyuti).
Because birth accords with one's feelings while death accords with one's intent,
both cases discuss only death. As for death through the breaking up of the aggregates (*prātibhinnaka-maraṇa*):
Those for whom the stomach is empty refer to those who are currently undergoing the experience of分段 (dufen-duan, segmented) birth-and-death;
those from the stage of Arhat downward are said to undergo 變易 (bianyi, transformative) birth-and-death.
"Up to the ultimate enlightenment" means understanding that there are no two kinds of places for birth and death.
This refers to the section below "the two kinds of death."
To explain further, the Tathāgata stated the reason for [the term] "ultimate":
because they have severed death in segments,
he said that for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, birth and death are exhausted.
Because one has attained the realization of the remaining fruits,
it is said that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established.
Because ordinary persons and gods do not give rise to untainted resolve (*anāsrava-adhimukti*), it is said that they have not yet distinguished [the truth].
Regarding the seven types of individuals— namely, those in the three fruits and four stages of realization— it is because they have not yet exhausted their original [defilements].
As for what was previously unaccomplished,
only the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have exhausted the three realms of conditioned existence as afflictions.
It is said that what was to be done has been accomplished;
the afflictions severed by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas can no longer cause the practitioner to receive further rebirths within the three realms.
Therefore, it is said that there is no further existence.
The Tathāgata speaks of performing the ultimate task while abiding herein.
From this point downward, there is a specific explanation for why Śrīmālā has not yet reached the ultimate.
The statement below does not mean that all afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted,
nor does it mean that all future births have been exhausted; rather,
it is said that there will be no further existence.

It is not that the Truth of the Accumulation (samudaya-satya), which consists of all afflictions, does not perish unless they are exhausted; nor is it that the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), which consists of all suffering of rebirth, is not grave unless it is exhausted.
Why is this? Because there are afflictions below [this level].
The second section clarifies the distinction between the two types of afflictions.
Within this, there are five textual passages that elucidate the meaning.
The first begins from the passage "What are the two? and so forth.
The beginningless ground of ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) and the two kinds of afflictions differ in their essential nature and root.
From the second section, starting from the passage "World-Honored One, these four grounds...
and below, it is explained that they possess the most powerful force, and their functions and powers are each distinct.

The third section, from "Furthermore, as with grasping as a condition" onwards, concludes by clarifying that there is a distinction between the two types of afflictions that moisten rebirth within the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
The fourth section begins from "Arhats in their final body, Bodhisattvas... and so forth.
The section from "Having attained liberation" up to "the taste" explains the distinction between the two types of knowledge.
The fifth section, from "Because the ground of ignorance has not been severed" onwards,
concludes with the Lion’s Roar of Wisdom, clarifying that the severance of fetters belongs to the Tathāgata.
Regarding the two kinds of afflictions:
the first is the affliction of the four abodes,
and the second is the delusion of ignorance.
What are these two?
The first is the abiding ground, as explained below;
the second is the arising of afflictions.
The initial arising of a single thought that is capable of producing [subsequent states] is called the "ground" (bhūmi).
That which causes these subsequent states to continue in an uninterrupted succession is called "abiding" (sthiti).
Because it serves as the ground for this abiding, it is termed the "ground of abiding" (sthiti-bhūmi).
Thus, each of these five locations has two aspects:
the dwelling and the ground.
There are four types of dwellings and grounds.
The following provides a separate explanation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.

Because the afflictions of the three realms—namely, those of the *darśana-heya* (to be abandoned by insight)—possess the characteristics of being coarse, heavy, and productive of rebirth, they are severed simultaneously upon the attainment of insight; therefore, they are grouped together as a single *anuśaya-sthāna* (abiding ground).
The coarse craving of the lower realm is called the ground of abiding in desire-love (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*).
Craving for the form realm is termed form-love (*rūparāga*).
And craving for the formless realm is explained as the ground of abiding in existence-love (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*).
When all four of these afflictions arise together in the higher realms,
they are all termed "transcending afflictions" (*samatikkama-kilesa*).
This is because the four minds share a single object and collectively achieve functional efficiency.
This refers to the association with momentary mind (*kṣaṇika-citta*).
As for the "mind-dissociated" (*citta-viprayukta*) factors mentioned by the World-Honored One,
they refer to the afflictions existing outside the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
That which is beginningless is the non-arising of the spiritual consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Once it has arisen, it relies upon objects;
this failure to clearly comprehend the objects upon which it relies is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there is nothing prior to it, it is called "beginningless.
To penetrate this single thought of ignorance that can give rise to subsequent states is called "ground" (bhūmi).
That subsequent afflictions arise and continue without interruption is called "abiding" (sthiti).
Because it serves as the ground for the abiding [of afflictions], it is called the "ground of the abiding of ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
The subsequent afflictions that arise from this are termed "arising" (*utthāna*) afflictions.
Because these arisings manifest *saṃkhyeya* (Ganges-sand-like) merits, they are called "Ganges-sand-like afflictions."
Thus, that which is above the myriad practices is called the "superior afflictions.
This continuity proceeds and gradually becomes coarser, approaching the three realms;
it is the initial arising of a single thought-moment of delusion that lacks manifest characteristics.
This is then considered the ground of abiding in craving (*tṛṣṇā-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Subsequently, that which arises from the back of this single thought-moment is called the arising of afflictions (*kleśa-utthāna*).
In this manner, it gradually becomes coarser and approaches the category of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).
It resembles the afflictions of the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, when one first gives rise to a single thought of the form realm, that itself constitutes the ground for abiding in craving for form (*rūparāga*).
Subsequently, from this, based on that single thought, the arising of afflictions occurs.
Even down to a single moment of thought in the desire realm is called the "ground of abiding in desire-attachment.
That which subsequently arises from the feet upward is called the "arising of afflictions.
In this way, the coarse [mind] of the desire realm is able to seek out and pursue objects.
Initially, the view of a self in the body constitutes the "ground-abiding view of one place" (*ekadeśasthāna-dṛṣṭi-pṛthivī*).
Furthermore, that which arises subsequently is also considered its origination.
In this way, there are the afflictions of the five ground-abidings (*pañca-pṛthivī-sthāna-kleśa*).
Within the three realms, because the four types of consciousness share the same object, they can be said to be associated in a single moment (*kṣaṇa-samprayukta*).
Beyond the three realms, the preceding and succeeding moments of mind are all non-apprehending;
since there is no distinction between the four types of consciousness, it is said that the mind is not associated (*citta-asamprayukta*).
It is the ground of abiding ignorance (avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi) from beginningless time.
Alternatively, according to the sūtras and śāstras, it may be explained as the non-abiding consciousness (anāśrita-vijñāna).
This is sometimes considered subtle and is thus termed the ground of abiding ignorance.
From the mind of perception and feeling up to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the dormant, indeterminate states constitute the *saṃsāra* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
from within the mind of the aggregate of formations, one single latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*) is extracted.
The coarse refers to the desire realm;
the intermediate refers to craving for the form realm;
and the subtle refers to craving for the formless realm.
The five views and the ten latent tendencies (anuśaya) are grouped together as the "abiding ground of views" (dṛṣṭi-sthānīya).
According to this interpretation, because the craving within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) may arise again,
it is said to be associated with moments (kṣaṇa-samprayukta).
Thus, the retribution and experience are determined by the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because the five consciousnesses cannot arise repeatedly,
it is said that they are "non-associated with the mind."
This refers to the ground of beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
"World-Honored One, as for the power of these four grounds of abiding"—
this second section clarifies that the functional power of the afflictions differs [from that of the ground of ignorance].
These four stages of abiding encompass the afflictions of the three realms.
The "higher afflictions" refer to the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Compared to these two types, the stage of abiding in ignorance is such that no calculation or analogy can possibly reach it.
This clarifies that the branches and twigs are not like the root; the afflictions of the lower realms do not reach the higher stages.

Thus, regarding the power of the "ground of abiding in ignorance" (avidyā-vāsabhūmi), the World-Honored One has reversed the sequence by taking the fundamental as the beginning and the derivative as the end, and the superior as the lower.
For example, the evil Māra Pāpīyas represents the afflictions of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*);
the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*) represent the afflictions of the four grounds of abiding that are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and the physical strength, power, and lifespan represent their functional efficacy.
This refers to sovereign excellence.
Thus, when this ground of the abiding of ignorance is combined with the power of the evil Māra Pāpīyān, it becomes even more formidable.
Combining these with the aforementioned power and function constitutes "having craving.
As for the "four stages of abiding" (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*), combining them with the sovereign devas whose power is most supreme constitutes the "superior excellence above."
In the near term, it serves as a basis for afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
furthermore, in the long run, it enables the four types of afflictions within the three realms to endure for a long time.
As for the statement that Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas cannot sever them:
In this context, it has not yet been clarified that the path of abandonment is unable to sever [afflictions] because the power of the higher ignorance-afflictions is so strong.
It can be severed only by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom. [The passage] beginning with "World-Honored One, below this...
concludes that the power of ignorance is strong. [The passage] beginning with "World-Honored One, there is 'appropriation' as a condition... [follows].
Third, it clarifies that there is a distinction regarding the moisture of afflictions for the production of existence (*bhava*).
"External conditions" refers to the single branch of grasping (*upādāna*) singled out from within the twelve links of dependent origination.
"The cause of tainted karma" refers to...
It also explains that one takes up the "existence" (*bhava*) link within the twelve links of dependent origination to give rise to the three realms of existence.
Within dependent origination, the "existence" link arises from the desire to receive a body in the three realms;
with craving and grasping as conditions and outflows (*āsrava*) as causes, existence comes to be.
Regarding "and thus one is born into the three realms of existence":
since the causes and conditions have been fully assembled, one receives a body within the three worlds; therefore, it is said that one is born into the three realms of existence.
This clarifies the method of taking birth upon the four stages of abiding (*vihāra*).
Hereafter, the method by which ignorance moistens the body will be explained.
In that state, wisdom becomes increasingly luminous and the afflictions gradually diminish.
The former [explanation] concerns the cause that brings about the subsequent [result],
while the latter allows for the presence of accompanying characteristics from the outset, or rather, it refers to its relationship with that wisdom;
this is because they mutually support one another despite being of different categories.
It is said that untainted karma takes the ground of the abiding of ignorance as its condition;
it may also take the realization that the three realms are truly empty as its cause.
Because one is born there,
it is said that untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*) is the cause;
this refers to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It must be due to afflictions (*kleśa*).
From the stage of Arhat downward, those who emerge from the cycle of birth and death are severed.
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), because there is only the transformation of the essence of gnosis (*jñāna*), it is called the "mind-made body" (*manomayakāya*).
These three stages constitute birth-and-death through segmentation (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*).
As for those three types, even beyond the three realms, there are those who can complete their births and return to the Path;
these are the persons of transformational birth (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), regarding whom one may also discuss birth-and-death through segmentation.
Within the three realms, the path of cultivation that is untainted (anāsrava) shatters and disperses birth and death;
at this time, it does not break [the seeds], nor does it moisten those for future transformation and rebirth,
and thus it is not included during the stage of affliction.
Therefore, the subsequent mention of "uncontaminated karma" and its arising also refers,
by remote dependence, to the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (avidyā-vāsabhūmi) as its condition and to the four types of uncontaminated understanding (anāsrava-jñāna).
Furthermore, by means of the afflictions of the four stages of abiding, one is moistened for rebirth and receives a body;
this is obtained as a result upon fruition.
Therefore, there are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
And as for the three realms and the untainted [dharmas],
due to the ground of the abiding of ignorance,
they possess this object-condition; it is not that they lack an object-condition.
World-Honored One, from this "ground of abiding in craving" downward,
one may again perform a comparative analysis;
for the afflictions of the lower levels do not reach those of the higher levels.
This means that it does not share the same causal karma as ignorance (*avidyā*).
From the passage "the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is distinct" onwards,
it can be said that the afflictions of this ground are also superior.
Regarding the afflictions of the lower realms that are severed at the stage of Buddhahood:
it is either because their karma is clearly severed, or it is to clarify that the power of these delusions is strong.
It has not yet been clarified which [afflictions] are severed at the stage of Buddhahood through mantras.
Because it is extinguished through understanding, it is said to be that which can be severed by the wisdom of bodhi. Why is this?
It is because only the wisdom of bodhi can eliminate it; the two vehicles cannot extinguish it.

The passage below states that because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have not severed the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-kleśa*) and their delusions and outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted,
they do not attain the four kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*), nor do they exercise sovereign power, nor do they realize the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the question of what those who lack [the realization of] non-existence and whose afflictions and outflows are not yet exhausted are, the text below states that they are precisely those dwelling in the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*).

From "Guiding the World" onwards is the fourth section; the preceding text, within the context of the four conditions, explained the differences between the two types of birth-and-death and the exhaustion of afflictions.
From this point onward, there is a formal explanation of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
They are distinguished by means of four kinds of knowledge.

those things which all arhats and great-power bodhisattvas have never before attained.

Regarding the "empty Tathāgatagarbha":

Because they can be easily cast off, they are called "if released from" (*yadi vimukta*).
Because they can undergo transformation, they are called "if changed into" (*yadi vikṛta*).
Since the essence of such a dharma has not yet been specified,

This is intended to clarify that because the statement "the path is impermanent, suffering, and empty" is a general designation capable of subsuming what was previously taught as cessation, it does not overlap with and thus effectively subsumes those instances where cessation was taught without being explicitly termed impermanent, suffering, or empty.

Regarding the discussion of the single truth (*ekasatya*): although various passages throughout the preceding chapters mention the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*)—namely, that which is severed by the wisdom of enlightenment (*bodhijñāna*)—the specific details of these matters are readily understandable.

"Three are impermanent and one is permanent," and so forth.

rather, it would be a distinct [negation] of both.
However, having completed the explanation of the Single Truth (ekasatya), the text subsequently states that it is eternal.
This "reliance" is designated by the two characters for "peace and security" (an-wei).
Thus, it constitutes the single textual phrase "the reliance of peace and security," with no further distinctions.
From this point on, beginning with the Truth of Cessation, is the twelfth chapter.
The reason for coming here is as follows:
previously, it was clarified that the Tathāgatagarbha abides eternally within the single truth; however, people mistakenly believe it exists within the very body.
This [section] clarifies that such a view is a perversion of reality.
Furthermore, understanding that deviates from principle is termed "inversion," while knowledge arising in accordance with principle is designated as "reality.
Because inversion and reality are combined into a single chapter, [the following is stated].
This is called the "reality of inversion.
Regarding this Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it refers back to the previous chapter to introduce the present one.
"Transcending all objects of perception for the minds of sentient beings" means:
In order to clarify that the eternally abiding Truth of Cessation is a wondrous and transcendent realm,
it is said that he "surpasses all sentient beings.
At that time, the assembly believed this was because a Śrāvaka was capable of such understanding.
This teaching is also not within the cognitive domain of the wisdom of the two vehicles.

For example, the analogy of one born blind is used for the sake of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) to clarify that just as one born blind does not perceive blue or yellow, so too do ordinary beings not see the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya).
The phrase "a seven-day-old infant who does not see the solar disc" is a metaphor for the Śrāvakas;
it clarifies that although the infant has eyes, he does not see the sun.
Similarly, the two vehicles possess wisdom, yet they do not contemplate the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*). This constitutes the application of the metaphor.
Regarding the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering:
the conjunction of form and the solar disc is not an object of perception for the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings; it is like being born blind.
Furthermore, that it is "not the realm of the wisdom of the two vehicles" corresponds to the "infant.
Although it was stated above that ordinary beings are like those born blind, this was not yet explained;
the following clarifies that this is due to the perversions of the two views.
These two are topical headings (*mukha*).
"All arhats are thus pure" is explained as being like an infant;
for this reason, it is also established as a topical heading.
From "extreme views" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) onwards, the first chapter is explained.
Regarding the aforementioned "two views of ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*),
the first is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) and the second is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).
Within these two deviations from the Middle Way, they are termed "pervasive.
From here below, three cycles clarify the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
the first clarifies how the divine self (*puruṣa*) gives rise to these two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
In the lower realms, one gives rise to the view of annihilation;
in the upper realms, one gives rise to the view of permanence.
Furthermore, one may give rise to the views of annihilation or permanence regarding the body, or even regarding nirvana.
Regarding the third form among the eternalist views, one reckons permanence upon the impermanent mind;
thus, ordinary persons, through attachment to the false marks of the view of self within the five aggregates of clinging, give rise to these two types of views.
Within the five aggregates, one gives rise to a mind of deluded conceptualization and clings to the existence of a self (ātman).
To calculate [the self] as being apart from the aggregates is called the view of eternalism;
to calculate it as being identical to the aggregates is to produce the view of nihilism.
"To say that the forgetting of the arising of marks gives rise to two views is what is called 'extreme view' (antagrāhadṛṣṭi):
this summarizes its essential nature."
This refers to the two views concerning the distinct perception of forms.
From the passage "These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent" onwards, the second [view] arises:
that the bodies obtained through the various practices of the six realms of existence are subject to arising and ceasing, and are thus impermanent.
This means that the view of annihilationism arises from the conviction that there will be no further continuity.
As for the view that nirvāṇa is eternal, this refers to those who conceive of the body in the higher realms as being nirvāṇa and ultimately imperishable; such is the view of eternalism.
This is not right view; it is to form such a view with a mind that has forgotten all characteristics.
Regarding the various faculties of the body, this is the third [section].
One is unable to distinguish among those five faculties.
Regarding those who destroy existence through views pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nāstika*):
they give rise to nihilism because they do not perceive the sense of rebirth within the continuity of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka-saṃtati*),
and because they are ignorant regarding the cessation of the mental continuum.
Because one does not know that moments (kṣaṇa) pass away and perish, the view of permanence (śāśvata-dṛṣṭi) arises.
This clarifies the conceptualization of permanence within the mind.
This refers to the view of forgetfulness and delusion.
This is called the "forgetful view of conceptualization" because it collectively cites the three positions regarding annihilationism and eternalism.
Regarding that meaning:
as for those three views, they either exceed or fall short of the meaning of that Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The view of annihilationism is called "excessive," while the view of eternalism is called "insufficient.

The reason for this is that while there is a principle that a future constant fruit must necessarily exist, the view of annihilationism claims that once this body has been discarded, there will forever be no further continuity.
If that were so, it would flow into the fruit of permanence;
therefore, the views of annihilationism and eternalism in these three positions are all termed faults.
Now, one must ultimately either exhaust [the defilements] or fulfill the Vajra-mind with perfect excellence.
That [consciousness] remains serene and does not perish;
those who perceive it constantly take this very body to be the self and the spirit that does not transmigrate.
Because they do not wait for the subsequent diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), it is said that they do not attain it.
From "perversion" onwards,
the preceding second chapter is explained:
[it concerns] the arising of the notion of permanence within the five aggregates of clinging, which are impermanent.
To perceive a mark of pleasure within the eight sufferings of birth and death;
to perceive a mark of self within the false aggregates that lack a real self—
these are called inversions because they consist of the impure marks of affliction.
From all Arhats downward, this concludes the explanation of the third chapter’s sections.
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have either transcended the three realms or dissolved their forms within the state of ordinary beings; therefore, they are called "pure."
The truth of cessation is not within the scope of what is known by that [wisdom].
Regarding the "object of omniscience," the response body (nirmāṇakāya) is the object of true wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding that which is fundamentally not seen within the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body:

because one regards that Buddha of sixteen feet as having been born for the first time in the royal palace and as having truly passed away at the Twin Trees, it is said that he was "fundamentally not seen."
Up to this point, the inversion has been explained; from here on, the true reality will be discussed.
"There may be sentient beings" refers to Bodhisattvas of the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*).
"Because they believe the Buddha’s words" means they accord with the teachings of the Buddha who appears in a sixteen-foot form.

they produce such an understanding with respect to that dharmakāya;

Why is this? Why is it that the arising of these marks of permanence, bliss, self, and purity within that Dharma-body is not a perversion?
The following passage states: "The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is permanent, blissful, self, and pure; its affairs are ultimate."
Because one knows the [qualities of] permanence, self, bliss, and purity according to reality and does not contradict their true meaning, it is called "correct" (*samyak*).
One who gives rise to right view regarding the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* will certainly be able to succeed to the noble lineage; therefore, they are called a "true son" (*aurasa-putra*).
Because his understanding of permanence was not yet complete, it is said that he "obtained remaining wealth.

This pure wisdom is termed "pure" because it is eternally free from the three realms.

[The following explains:]

From this point downward, the lower stages are explained by means of the higher.

One who is not deluded regarding the Dharma is an Arhat.

Because those of the *śrāvaka* lineage attain the understanding of signlessness (*animitta*),
the World-Honored One taught the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

All [of these] are able to serve as a support for sentient beings.
