Regarding the passage beginning with "World-Honored One, birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*," and so forth:
Chapter Thirteen. Regarding the reason for coming here:

the preceding section clarified that when sentient beings are in a state of delusion regarding reality, they mistakenly believe that the principle (*tattva*) can be defiled, thereby becoming inverted with respect to that principle.
Now it is clarified that the essence and nature of the Tathāgatagarbha are luminously pure and exist beyond all afflictions; its intrinsic nature is pure.

Furthermore, the preceding explanation of various interpretations that contradict reason is termed "perverted conceptualization," whereas the knowledge arising from the principle of reality is termed "truth."
It is now clarified that the reason these virtues and evils do not cease is because they rely upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
For this reason, immediately following the discussion on the inversion of reality, the intrinsic purity of self-nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is explained.
World-Honored One, if birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, one should say that the continuity of birth and death persists;
why is it not severed? It is because of the *tathāgatagarbha*. If there were no *tathāgatagarbha*, [birth and death would be severed].
Since one birth and one death constitute a single transformation that fulfills the principle of attaining Buddhahood,
and because this continuity is uninterrupted, what is called "birth and death" is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within this chapter, there are three sections that clarify the meaning.
The first clarifies that the good and evil of birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The third begins from the passage "From the *tathāgatagarbha*... and so forth.
This clearly elucidates the obscuration of the intrinsically pure mind;
it may also be said that the *tathāgatagarbha* is not defiled by afflictions.
The third section, from "When he spoke this dharma that is difficult to understand" onwards, clarifies the Tathāgata’s confirmation and completion of the teaching.
Within the first section, there are also three passages.
The first clarifies that birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The second, beginning from "World-Honored One, if there were no *tathāgatagarbha*," clarifies that good and evil depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The third section, from "From the Tathāgata-garbha of the World-Honored One" down to "it is not the self," clarifies the differences from non-Buddhist outsiders.
It states that because of the Tathāgata-garbha, the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is said to be unknowable.
Precisely because the Tathāgatagarbha lies behind the diamond-heart,
sentient beings are unable to manifest its function in the present. Consequently,
the essence of sentient beings is not self-sustaining, and they undergo birth and death moment by moment.
Thus, because the past is boundless and the future is infinite,
it is said that the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is unknowable.
It is because the World-Honored One possesses the *tathāgatagarbha* that he speaks of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Because the Tathāgatagarbha exists within sentient beings in both the present and the future,
there are numerous cycles of birth and death;
since this statement accords with reality, it is well-spoken.
From here below, the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is explained.
Second, the *tathāgatagarbha* is elucidated.
Third, regarding how birth and death depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*: herein, "birth and death" refers specifically to the death of the preceding body.
Regarding the statement that "in this present life, as the stages of birth unfold, one does not receive the arising of various sensations through the sense faculties":
these five aggregates are called "various sensations" because they are received and obtained from karma;
they are called "disappearance" because the five aggregates perish and are lost.
"Succession" refers to the arising of the present body.
Regarding "succession does not arise from the reception of the faculties":
because the present body exists within the past form and precedes what follows, it is said that succession does not [arise] from them.
Because the preceding body is obtained through karma separated from its form, it is said that "the arising of the faculties occurs without [a prior] reception.
This is called "birth and death," which refers to the present body.
"World-Honored One, these two dharmas—birth and death—are the Tathāgatagarbha."
These two phenomena of birth and death are based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The passage beginning with "In accordance with worldly convention,
there is death and there is birth" clarifies that one attains birth in the future through the death of the present body.
The three periods of time clarify birth and death.
Because one wishes to clarify the continuity across the three periods of time, the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be known.
That which dies in the present body is the destruction of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Regarding "the arising of a subsequent body," this refers to the emergence of new sense-faculties (*indriya*).
To say "one dies" means the sense-faculties perish;
to say "one is born" means new sense-faculties emerge.
"It is not the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is not that the Tathāgatagarbha has death or birth" is intended to clarify that the eternally abiding essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is without transition or change.
Therefore, because the Tathāgatagarbha is eternally abiding,
it serves as the "basis," providing a foundation for saṃsāra;
it serves as the "support," maintaining the continuity of saṃsāra so that it does not disperse.
That which establishes [the nature] cannot be severed.
As for the World-Honored One’s statement that it is "not to be abandoned," the essence of the treasury is eternally abiding and thus cannot be severed or discarded.
That which is not liberated is not easily liberated;
that which is not different cannot be altered.
Of such a dharma, what is meant by "inferior"? It refers to the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
This correctly elucidates the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha.
From the beginningless cycle of birth and death, it has been its locus.
As for the "severing and liberation" by the World-Honored One:
Birth and death are impermanent, capable of being severed and escaped from;
that which is different can be made to undergo transformation.
As for "the external," it refers to the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, which exists outside of these conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) such as severance, escape, and difference.
That which is able to serve as the support and foundation for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
From this point onward, the World-Honored One clarifies that both good and evil depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.
To clarify that the phenomena of good and evil arise from the Tathāgatagarbha and give rise to birth and death, the cycle of transmigration is endless;
yet because the arising of wholesome dharmas accords with the Tathāgatagarbha, one may reverse the flow and exhaust the source.
In this context, it is because there exists a *tathāgatagarbha* that [the teaching] is established;
it is not established for those who lack understanding.
If the *tathāgatagarbha* did not exist, [the teaching] would not be established.
One must not weary of suffering nor seek nirvana with longing.

Why is this? Śāriputra, because those who lack the *tathāgatagarbha* cannot weary of suffering or seek nirvana. It is stated below that within these six consciousnesses and the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), wisdom does not plant manifold sufferings.
Because there is no *tathāgatagarbha*, the six consciousnesses arise based on the six sense organs; "mind" (*citta*) and "mental faculty" (*manas*) refer to the mental organ (*manendriya*).
"Dharma-wisdom" (*dharmajñāna*) refers to the empty understanding within the mental organ.

These seven dharmas transform and transform themselves until they cease; because they do not abide for even a single moment, it is said that the six consciousnesses and the mind do not plant the seeds of manifold sufferings.
Even the wisdom of dharmas cannot find cause for revulsion toward suffering, nor can it seek nirvana.
This explains by way of reverse order;
from "World-Honored One" onwards, it explains in direct order.
That the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit means it does not belong to the future.
That which does not arise does not belong to the present;
that which does not cease does not exist in the past.
This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is eternal.
The "seeds of the Dharma that produce manifold sufferings" refers to the six consciousnesses and the mind extensively giving rise to various evils.
"Joyfully seeking nirvāṇa" means that through the wisdom of the Dharma,
one attains weariness with suffering and joyfully seeks nirvāṇa.
The World-Honored One has already clarified that non-Buddhists and outsiders reckon the body to possess a self (*ātman*) that is immutable and indestructible.
Now, to clarify that the eternally abiding *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as what these people [reckon], he says, "It is not a self" and "not a sentient being."
Because it lies beyond all accumulated afflictions following the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), it is not within the realm of ordinary beings.
Those with inverted views perceive it as permanence;
those whose minds are disturbed by suffering hold the view of annihilation.
Regarding the second section, the "Dharmadhātu-garbha" (Treasury of the Dharma-realm) as taught by the World-Honored One:
it is called a "realm" (*dhātu*) because the eternal fruit of Buddhahood is distinct from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
It is named the "Dharma-body treasury" (*dharmakāya-garbha*) because its essence is fully endowed with all virtues.
It is called "supreme" because it transcends birth and death.
It is called the "naturally pure *tathāgatagarbha*" because its nature is luminous and pure, untainted by afflictions;
this is merely citing the text to clarify the meaning of being concealed and covered.
Regarding "adventitious afflictions" (*āgantuka-kleśa*):
they are called "adventitious" because they arise outside of the fundamental principle.
Regarding "superior afflictions": these are either these very [adventitious ones] or those that exist above the myriad practices (*sahasra-pratipatti*).
The Tathāgatagarbha is defiled by two kinds of afflictions;
this is the realm of the Tathāgatas and is not something that persons of inferior capacity can know.
From here on, the profound will be explained through the shallow.
Why is this? It is because it clarifies that if a moment exists in the present, the mind of affliction belongs to the past or the future;
therefore, it is said not to be defiled by afflictions.
Even a momentary unwholesome mind is not defiled by afflictions;
because a single moment of unwholesomeness exists while the present wholesome mind has already passed away,
it is likewise not defiled by afflictions.
Regarding "afflictions do not touch the mind":
it means that afflictions do not reach a wholesome mind, and as for "the wholesome mind does not touch afflictions," it means that the wholesome mind does not reach the afflictions.
What is meant by "how can one attain a defiled mind without contact with dharmas"?
Since they have never come into mutual contact, by what means could they be defiled?
The above clarifies that the emptiness of substantial dharmas is such that their own essence is inherently extinguished; thus, there is absolutely no mutual defilement.

From the perspective of the World-Honored One downward, because one grasps the continuity of provisional designations as a single unit, there is a continuity of stained characteristics for a hundred years that should give rise to superior or middling wholesome states;

however, because a middling or inferior unwholesome mind arises in the interim, a superior or middling wholesome mind cannot maintain its continuity, and is therefore termed a "preceding wholesome mind."
Now, because an evil mind is being produced, it is said that the mind is defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, one fully knows and sees that such a principle of non-attachment is the naturally pure self-nature.

Nor should there be separate textual passages [for each].

because there are three distinct types of true sons, they must be treated separately.

The passage beginning with "emitting supreme light" and below clarifies the teaching on its circulation.

Regarding "seven *tāla* trees high":
one arrow-shot distance is three hundred paces;

The preceding section has sought to encourage the upholding and dissemination [of this scripture] by first weighing its merits;
